title: Texas Agriculture Department Bars H-1B Employers From Its State Grants
excerpt: Commissioner Sid Miller's October 28 policy cuts businesses employing H-1B workers out of Texas Department of Agriculture grants and challenges other state officials to follow.
body:
• The Texas Department of Agriculture will no longer award its eligible grants to businesses that employ H-1B visa holders, Commissioner Sid Miller announced on October 28.
  • The bar covers grants the department administers itself; it does not apply to federal grant money, state-funded loan programs, or programs run for independent boards.
  • H-1B status itself is unchanged — this is a state funding condition, not a visa suspension. Texas had more than 41,000 H-1B recipients in fiscal 2025.
  • If your Texas business employs even degreed H-1B staff — scientists, engineers, analysts — check TDA grant eligibility before applying; the department has not yet published how compliance will be certified.

Texas businesses that employ H-1B visa holders will no longer be eligible for grants administered by the Texas Department of Agriculture (TDA), Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller announced on October 28. The policy extends Texas's campaign against the H-1B program from the state's own payroll to private employers seeking state money.

"Texas taxpayers work hard for their money. They deserve to know that their tax dollars are being used to create opportunities for Texans — not to subsidize businesses that choose foreign labor while Texans are ready and willing to work," Miller said in the department's announcement. "If a company wants taxpayer support, it should demonstrate a commitment to the people paying the bill. Texas workers should come first. Period."

"Governor Abbott has publicly declared that taxpayer-funded employment should prioritize Texans. I agree — and now it's time to turn that principle into action."

— Sid Miller, Texas Agriculture Commissioner

What the policy covers — and what it leaves open

The restriction applies to "eligible department-administered grants." It does not apply to TDA programs operated on behalf of independent boards, commissions or entities that set their own eligibility criteria, and it does not restrict federal grant funds or state-funded loan programs administered by the department.

Critical mechanics are still missing, as an analysis by Immigration Analytics points out: the announcement names no specific program, does not say how a business proves it employs no H-1B workers, whether a single H-1B employee anywhere on the payroll disqualifies the company, whether contractor-placed H-1B staff count, or what happens to grants already awarded. The policy also does not mention H-2A seasonal farmworker visas. Because H-1B covers specialty occupations that generally require a bachelor's degree — the USCIS definition — the businesses most exposed are larger operations employing scientists, engineers and analysts rather than family farms.

How this differs from Abbott's freeze

Texas has restricted H-1B before, but only as an employer. Governor Greg Abbott's January 27 directive ordered state agencies and public universities to file no new H-1B petitions without Texas Workforce Commission approval through May 31, 2027. Miller's move is different in kind: it uses state funding to shape whom private companies hire, and Miller framed it as a direct challenge to Abbott and every statewide elected official to apply the same test to their own grant and incentive programs.

The move lands on top of federal pressure. Under the September 2025 presidential proclamation described on the USCIS H-1B page, certain new H-1B petitions for beneficiaries outside the US must carry a $100,000 payment. Texas had more than 41,000 H-1B recipients in fiscal 2025, Axios reported, and Indian nationals make up the largest share of H-1B workers nationally — many of them in Texas technology, healthcare and research roles.

What to watch

Three things will decide how much this matters: TDA guidance spelling out certification and definitions; whether Abbott or other statewide officials adopt similar grant conditions, as Miller urged; and whether the policy survives Miller himself — he lost the March Republican primary, his term ends in January, and his successor will decide whether it stays. Legal challenges are possible on federal-preemption grounds, though courts generally give governments more room when they act as funders rather than regulators.
